## BNP Paribas Leadership Structure & Executive Committee

### Overview

BNP Paribas is a French multinational banking and financial services group headquartered in Paris. Its leadership is organized around a **General Management** team and a broader **Executive Committee** that together set and implement the Group's strategy. The Executive Committee meets at least once a week.

---

### General Management (6 members)

The General Management comprises the CEO, two Chief Operating Officers (COOs), and three Deputy Chief Operating Officers (DCOOs):

| Name | Role |
|------|------|
| **Jean-Laurent Bonnafé** | Director and Chief Executive Officer |
| **Yann Gérardin** | Chief Operating Officer — in charge of Corporate & Institutional Banking (CIB) |
| **Thierry Laborde** | Chief Operating Officer — in charge of Commercial, Personal Banking & Services (CPBS) |
| **Renaud Dumora** | Deputy Chief Operating Officer — in charge of Investment & Protection Services (IPS) |
| **Philippe Maillard** | Chief Operating Officer (Group COO) |
| *(6th General Management seat)* | *(see additional members below)* |

As CEO, **Jean-Laurent Bonnafé** bears responsibility for the management of the entire Group and is invested with extensive powers; all operational activities and Group functions fall under his direct responsibility.

---

### Full Executive Committee Members (as of April 2025, with subsequent updates through 2026)

Beyond the General Management, the Executive Committee includes **heads of business lines and central functions**. As of the most recent composition, the members are:

| Name | Responsibility |
|------|----------------|
| **Michael Anseeuw** | Director and CEO / Chairman of the Executive Board, BNP Paribas Fortis |
| **Marc Camus** | Chief Information Officer |
| **Charlotte Dennery** | Director and CEO, BNP Paribas Personal Finance |
| **Elena Goitini** | CEO of BNL (Italy) |
| **Élise Hermant** | Head of Communications |
| **Yannick Jung** | Head of CIB Global Banking |
| **Pauline Leclerc-Glorieux** | Director and CEO, BNP Paribas Cardif |
| **Isabelle Loc** | Head of Commercial & Personal Banking in France |
| **Stéphanie Maarek** | Head of Compliance |
| **Lars Machenil** | Chief Financial Officer |
| **Olivier Osty** | Head of CIB Global Markets |
| **Sandro Pierri** | CEO of BNP Paribas Asset Management (joined the Executive Committee on 30 March 2026) |
| **Anne Pointet** | Head of Company Engagement |
| **Frank Roncey** | Chief Risk Officer |
| **Sarah Roussel** | Head of Human Resources (appointed 1 July 2026, succeeding Sofia Merlo) |
| **Gilles Zeitoun** | *(Executive Committee member)* |

---

### Key Responsibilities of the Executive Committee

- **Strategy setting and implementation**: The Executive Committee sets and implements BNP Paribas' overall strategy, driving the Group's strategic plan to consolidate European leadership and grow profitably.
- **Operational oversight**: All operational activities and Group functions are coordinated through the committee, with the CEO holding ultimate responsibility.
- **Sustainable economy transition**: The committee coordinates the Group's efforts to accelerate the transition to a sustainable economic model and support clients on this path.
- **Diversity and governance**: In 2024, 42% of Executive Committee members were women, exceeding the Group's target of 40% by 2025.
- **Weekly meetings**: The Executive Committee convenes at least once a week to ensure close coordination across business lines and functions.

---

### Recent Changes (2026)

- **Sandro Pierri** joined the Executive Committee on 30 March 2026 as CEO of the newly unified BNP Paribas Asset Management, reporting to Renaud Dumora. This appointment reflects the strategic positioning of asset management as a growth engine under the Group's 2030 strategic plan.
- **Sarah Roussel** was appointed Group Head of Human Resources effective 1 July 2026, succeeding Sofia Merlo, and joined the Executive Committee reporting to COO Philippe Maillard.

explainability.content: BNP Paribas’ leadership is organized around a General Management team consisting of the CEO, two COOs and three DCOOs, which together form the core of the Executive Committee.
Jean‑Laurent Bonnafé, as Director and Chief Executive Officer, holds ultimate responsibility for the Group’s management and all operational activities and functions.

The Executive Committee includes the General Management members plus heads of business lines and central functions, totaling 14‑15 additional members such as Michael Anseeuw, Marc Camus, Charlotte Dennery, Elena Goitini, etc.
The Committee meets at least once a week to ensure coordination across the Group’s businesses and functions.

Its key responsibilities are to set and implement the Group’s overall strategy, oversee all operational activities, drive the transition to a sustainable economy, and monitor diversity and governance targets.
In 2024, 42 % of Executive Committee members were women, surpassing the 40 % target for 2025.
On 30 March 2026, Sandro Pierri joined the Executive Committee as CEO of BNP Paribas Asset Management, reporting to Deputy COO Renaud Dumora.
Effective 1 July 2026, Sarah Roussel became Group Head of Human Resources and joined the Executive Committee, reporting to COO Philippe Maillard.

{"content":"## Yann Gérardin — COO of BNP Paribas, Corporate & Institutional Banking (CIB)

### Current Role

Since **1 September 2025**, Yann Gérardin serves as **Chief Operating Officer (COO) of BNP Paribas** and **Executive Chairman of Corporate & Institutional Banking (CIB)**. He is one of two COOs in BNP Paribas' General Management, which is composed of a CEO, two COOs, and three Deputy COOs.

### Responsibilities

In his capacity as COO and Executive Chairman of CIB, Gérardin's responsibilities encompass:

- **Overall leadership of the CIB division**, which serves two core client franchises:
  - **Corporate clients** — offering cash management, trade finance, financing products (including structured, specialised, and long-term financing), and advisory services.
  - **Institutional clients** — encompassing securities services, prime brokerage, and repo businesses.
- **Direct oversight of Global Markets**, including Sales, Structuring & Trading, and regional Capital Markets heads (EMEA, APAC, Americas) reporting to him.
- **Strategic transformation** of CIB — industrialising, rationalising, and digitalising business models to deliver holistic, added-value solutions to clients.
- **Building the bridge between corporate and institutional franchises**, leveraging processing businesses at the base and financing capabilities at the top of each pillar.
- **Positioning BNP Paribas CIB as the European reference partner with global reach**, with a strong presence in Europe, the Americas, and Asia-Pacific.

### Career Progression at BNP Paribas

| Year | Role |
|------|------|
| 1987 | Joined BNP; created the Equity Derivatives business |
| 1999 | Appointed Global Head of Equity Derivatives at BNP Paribas |

| 2014 | Head of Corporate & Institutional Banking (CIB) |
| 2018 | Deputy Chief Operating Officer of BNP Paribas Group, in charge of CIB |
| 2021 | Chief Operating Officer of BNP Paribas, Head of CIB |
| 2025 | Chief Operating Officer of BNP Paribas and Executive Chairman of CIB |

### Education

Yann Gérardin graduated from **Institut d'Études Politiques** and **École des Hautes Études Commerciales (HEC)**.

### Recognition

## Yann Gérardin — COO of BNP Paribas, Corporate & Institutional Banking (CIB)

### Current Role

Since **1 September 2025**, Yann Gérardin serves as **Chief Operating Officer (COO) of BNP Paribas** and **Executive Chairman of Corporate & Institutional Banking (CIB)**. He is one of two COOs in BNP Paribas' General Management, which is composed of a CEO, two COOs, and three Deputy COOs.

### Responsibilities

In his capacity as COO and Executive Chairman of CIB, Gérardin's responsibilities encompass:

- **Overall leadership of the CIB division**, which serves two core client franchises:
  - **Corporate clients** — offering cash management, trade finance, financing products (including structured, specialised, and long-term financing), and advisory services.
  - **Institutional clients** — encompassing securities services, prime brokerage, and repo businesses.
- **Direct oversight of Global Markets**, including Sales, Structuring & Trading, and regional Capital Markets heads (EMEA, APAC, Americas) reporting to him.
- **Strategic transformation** of CIB — industrialising, rationalising, and digitalising business models to deliver holistic, added-value solutions to clients.
- **Building the bridge between corporate and institutional franchises**, leveraging processing businesses at the base and financing capabilities at the top of each pillar.
- **Positioning BNP Paribas CIB as the European reference partner with global reach**, with a strong presence in Europe, the Americas, and Asia-Pacific.

### Career Progression at BNP Paribas

| Year | Role |
|------|------|
| 1987 | Joined BNP; created the Equity Derivatives business |
| 1999 | Appointed Global Head of Equity Derivatives at BNP Paribas |
| 2005 | Head of Equity and Equity Derivatives division (Commodities Derivatives integrated the same year) |
| 2011 | Member of the BNP Paribas Group Executive Committee |
| 2014 | Head of Corporate & Institutional Banking (CIB) |
| 2018 | Deputy Chief Operating Officer of BNP Paribas Group, in charge of CIB |
| 2021 | Chief Operating Officer of BNP Paribas, Head of CIB |
| 2025 | Chief Operating Officer of BNP Paribas and Executive Chairman of CIB |

### Education

Yann Gérardin graduated from **Institut d'Études Politiques** and **École des Hautes Études Commerciales (HEC)**.

### Recognition

He received the **Lifetime Achievement Award** from *Risk* magazine, recognising his outstanding contributions to derivatives, risk management, quantitative finance, and regulation over his career.

## Thierry Laborde — COO, Commercial, Personal Banking & Services (CPBS) at BNP Paribas

**Thierry Laborde** (born 1960) is the **Chief Operating Officer (COO) and Deputy CEO of BNP Paribas**, in charge of the **Commercial, Personal Banking & Services (CPBS)** division. He was appointed to this role in 2021.

### Career Background

- Began his career in 1982 at Banque Nationale de Paris.
- Held progressively senior roles in French Retail Banking, including Head of the Strasbourg Branch Group (1999–2001), Head of the Marseilles Branch Group (2001–2006), and Head of Local Networks (until 2008).
- Served as **Chairman and CEO of BNP Paribas Personal Finance** (2008–2015), overseeing the group's consumer credit solutions.
- In 2011, joined the BNP Paribas Group Executive Committee.
- In 2015, appointed **Deputy Chief Operating Officer and Head of Domestic Markets**, encompassing retail banking networks in France, Italy, Belgium, and Luxembourg, plus specialized businesses (Arval, Leasing Solutions, Personal Investors, Nickel).
- In **2021**, appointed **Chief Operating Officer of BNP Paribas, in charge of CPBS**.

### CPBS Division — Scope and Responsibilities

As COO heading CPBS, Thierry Laborde oversees one of BNP Paribas's three main operating divisions. His responsibilities include:

- **Commercial & Personal Banking networks** across the euro zone — including France, Italy, Belgium, Luxembourg, and the integrated commercial & personal banking model being rolled out across several Mediterranean countries, Türkiye, and Eastern Europe.
- **Specialized businesses** within CPBS, notably:
  - **BNP Paribas Personal Finance** (European leader in consumer credit)
  - **Arval** (vehicle leasing and fleet management)
  - **BNP Paribas Leasing Solutions** (equipment and technology financing)
  - **Nickel** (digital banking)
- **Services offered** under CPBS include: financing and equipment leasing, lending, investment products, financial and non-financial services, mobility solutions, digital banking, current accounts, savings products, bancassurance, insurance products and services, and consumer loans.
- **Leadership oversight**: Key executives report directly to Laborde, including the heads of Commercial & Personal Banking in France, BNP Paribas Personal Finance, BNP Paribas Leasing Solutions, and the Deputy CEO in charge of euro zone commercial banks.

### Reporting Line

Thierry Laborde reports to **Jean-Laurent Bonnafé**, Managing Director and CEO of BNP Paribas, and is a member of the Group's Executive Committee and General Management.

{"content":"## Jean-Laurent Bonnafé — CEO of BNP Paribas

### Background

Jean-Laurent Bonnafé (born 14 July 1961 in Albi, France) is a French banking executive who serves as Director and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of BNP Paribas. He is a graduate of École Polytechnique and École des Mines.

### Career Path

- Began his career in the French civil service, first as a Senior Officer at the Ministry of Industry, then as Technical Advisor to the Minister of Trade and Industry.
- Joined BNP in **1993** as a Senior Investment Banker.
- Appointed **Head of Strategy and Development** in 1997.
- Led the **post-merger integration** of BNP and Paribas following their merger in 2000.
- Appointed **Head of French Retail Banking** in 2002, joining the BNP Paribas Executive Committee.
- Named **Managing Director of BNL** (Banca Nazionale del Lavoro) in 2006 after its integration into BNP Paribas.
- Became **Chief Operating Officer (COO)** of BNP Paribas in 2008, with responsibility for the Group's Retail Banking activities.
- Served as **CEO of Fortis Bank** from May 2009 to February 2011, overseeing its integration.
- Appointed **Group CEO** of BNP Paribas at the end of 2011.

### CEO Responsibilities and Duties

As Chief Executive Officer, Jean-Laurent Bonnafé bears responsibility for the **overall management of the BNP Paribas Group** and is invested with the most extensive powers for this purpose. Specifically:

- **All operational activities and Group functions** fall under his direct responsibility.
- The General Management structure under him comprises two Chief Operating Officers and three Deputy Chief Operating Officers.
- He oversees BNP Paribas's three core business divisions: **Retail Banking**, **Investment Solutions**, and **Corporate & Institutional Banking (CIB)**.
- He leads the Group's strategic direction, including capital allocation, technology transformation, and cost discipline.
- He is responsible for strengthening the Group's **capital and liquidity buffers** — the equity base has more than doubled since the 2008 crisis, and the liquidity buffer has grown from approximately €60 billion to around €300 billion.
- He oversees **compliance and risk management**, including anti-money laundering, foreign sanctions compliance (annual spending rising from ~€7 million to ~€200 million), and **cybersecurity** (~€400 million per year).
- He champions the Group's **sustainability and diversity** commitments, including participation in initiatives such as the UN's HeForShe campaign and responsible investment efforts.

### Mandate Extension

In May 2025, BNP Paribas shareholders confirmed Bonnafé for another three-year term as director and voted to raise the CEO age limit from 65 to 68, enabling the then-63-year-old to remain at the helm until 2028. This makes him one of Europe's longest-serving bank CEOs.

### Other Roles and Memberships

- Board member of **Carrefour**
- Member of the **Association Française des Entreprises pour l'Environnement (EpE)**
- Member of the board of **Fondation la France s'engage**

## Jean-Laurent Bonnafé — CEO of BNP Paribas

### Background

Jean-Laurent Bonnafé (born 14 July 1961 in Albi, France) is a French banking executive who serves as Director and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of BNP Paribas. He is a graduate of École Polytechnique and École des Mines.

### Career Path

- Began his career in the French civil service, first as a Senior Officer at the Ministry of Industry, then as Technical Advisor to the Minister of Trade and Industry.
- Joined BNP in **1993** as a Senior Investment Banker.
- Appointed **Head of Strategy and Development** in 1997.
- Led the **post-merger integration** of BNP and Paribas following their merger in 2000.
- Appointed **Head of French Retail Banking** in 2002, joining the BNP Paribas Executive Committee.
- Named **Managing Director of BNL** (Banca Nazionale del Lavoro) in 2006 after its integration into BNP Paribas.
- Became **Chief Operating Officer (COO)** of BNP Paribas in 2008, with responsibility for the Group's Retail Banking activities.
- Served as **CEO of Fortis Bank** from May 2009 to February 2011, overseeing its integration.
- Appointed **Group CEO** of BNP Paribas at the end of 2011.

### CEO Responsibilities and Duties

As Chief Executive Officer, Jean-Laurent Bonnafé bears responsibility for the **overall management of the BNP Paribas Group** and is invested with the most extensive powers for this purpose. Specifically:

- **All operational activities and Group functions** fall under his direct responsibility.
- The General Management structure under him comprises two Chief Operating Officers and three Deputy Chief Operating Officers.
- He oversees BNP Paribas's three core business divisions: **Retail Banking**, **Investment Solutions**, and **Corporate & Institutional Banking (CIB)**.
- He leads the Group's strategic direction, including capital allocation, technology transformation, and cost discipline.
- He is responsible for strengthening the Group's **capital and liquidity buffers** — the equity base has more than doubled since the 2008 crisis, and the liquidity buffer has grown from approximately €60 billion to around €300 billion.
- He oversees **compliance and risk management**, including anti-money laundering, foreign sanctions compliance (annual spending rising from ~€7 million to ~€200 million), and **cybersecurity** (~€400 million per year).
- He champions the Group's **sustainability and diversity** commitments, including participation in initiatives such as the UN's HeForShe campaign and responsible investment efforts.

### Mandate Extension

In May 2025, BNP Paribas shareholders confirmed Bonnafé for another three-year term as director and voted to raise the CEO age limit from 65 to 68, enabling the then-63-year-old to remain at the helm until 2028. This makes him one of Europe's longest-serving bank CEOs.

### Other Roles and Memberships

- Board member of **Carrefour**
- Member of the **Association Française des Entreprises pour l'Environnement (EpE)**
- Member of the board of **Fondation la France s'engage**
- Board involvement with **Banca Nazionale del Lavoro (BNL)**

The General Management structure includes a CEO, two COOs and three Deputy COOs, and the CEO holds extensive powers over all operational activities and Group functions, establishing his overall management responsibility.
As CEO, Bonnafé directly oversees the three core business divisions—Retail Banking, Investment Solutions, and Corporate & Institutional Banking—defining the scope of his duties.
He is responsible for strategic direction, including capital allocation, technology transformation, and cost discipline, as part of his CEO duties.
His role includes strengthening capital and liquidity buffers, compliance and risk management (AML, sanctions, cybersecurity), and promoting sustainability and diversity initiatives.
Shareholders confirmed his appointment for an additional three‑year term and raised the CEO age limit to 68, extending his tenure and underscoring the continuity of his responsibilities.

As far as his own bank is concerned, Bonnafé is relatively satisfied with the business model and how it is developing.

“We are attracting talent; we are diversifying; we are disciplined,” he says. He thinks the bank is keeping abreast of the opportunity technology brings to lower costs by sharing platforms for activities such as payments that may not be essential to the bank’s core role as a financier, adviser and risk manager. [...] Since the 2008 crisis, says Bonnafé, banks have had to ramp up their capital and liquidity buffers, and spend much more on anti-money laundering compliance and foreign sanctions, as well as cybersecurity. BNP Paribas’ equity base has more than doubled, while its liquidity buffer has increased from about €60 billion to about €300 billion. Its annual compliance spending has risen from about €7 million to around €200 million; and it now spends about €400 million a year on cybersecurity. [...] “To become a banker you need to study maths and history, because you have cycles,” he says. “Part of it is metrics and part of it is just human nature. Behind Brexit, for example, there’s human nature. When you start to believe that a certain situation is definitively under control, then maybe you find yourself at the beginning of an issue. You should have a scientific approach in banking, but it should also be linked to the way human beings feel.”

## BNP Paribas Leadership Organizational Structure and Responsibilities

BNP Paribas, a French multinational banking and financial services group headquartered in Paris, has a well-defined leadership structure centered around **General Management** and an **Executive Committee**.

---

### **General Management Structure**

The General Management consists of **six members**:
- **1 Chief Executive Officer (CEO)**
- **2 Chief Operating Officers (COOs)**
- **3 Deputy Chief Operating Officers (Deputy COOs)**

---

### **Key Leadership Members and Their Responsibilities**

#### **1. Jean-Laurent Bonnafé – Director and Chief Executive Officer**

**Responsibilities:**
- Bears ultimate responsibility for the **overall management of the BNP Paribas Group**
- Invested with the most extensive powers; **all operational activities and Group functions** fall under his direct responsibility
- Oversees the Group's three core business divisions: Retail Banking, Investment Solutions, and Corporate & Institutional Banking
- Leads strategic direction, including capital allocation, technology transformation, and cost discipline
- Responsible for strengthening capital and liquidity buffers (equity base more than doubled since 2008; liquidity buffer grew from ~€60 billion to ~€300 billion)
- Oversees compliance and risk management, including anti-money laundering, foreign sanctions compliance (annual spending rising from ~€7 million to ~€200 million), and cybersecurity (~€400 million per year)
- Champions sustainability and diversity commitments

**Background:** Graduate of École Polytechnique and École des Mines; joined BNP in 1993; appointed Group CEO in 2011; mandate extended until 2028.

---

#### **2. Yann Gérardin – Chief Operating Officer and Executive Chairman of Corporate & Institutional Banking (CIB)**

**Responsibilities (since September 1, 2025):**
- **Overall leadership of the CIB division**, serving two core client franchises:
  - **Corporate clients:** cash management, trade finance, financing products (structured, specialized, long-term), and advisory services
  - **Institutional clients:** securities services, prime brokerage, and repo businesses
- **Direct oversight of Global Markets**, including Sales, Structuring & Trading, with regional Capital Markets heads (EMEA, APAC, Americas) reporting to him
- **Strategic transformation of CIB:** industrializing, rationalizing, and digitalizing business models to deliver holistic, added-value solutions
- Positioning BNP Paribas CIB as the **European reference partner with global reach**

**Background:** Joined BNP in 1987; created the Equity Derivatives business; appointed Head of CIB in 2014; promoted to COO in 2021; graduate of Institut d'Études Politiques and HEC.

---

#### **3. Thierry Laborde – Chief Operating Officer in charge of Commercial, Personal Banking & Services (CPBS)**

**Responsibilities (appointed 2021):**
- Oversees the **CPBS division**, one of BNP Paribas's three main operating divisions
- **Commercial & Personal Banking networks** across the euro zone: France, Italy, Belgium, Luxembourg, and integrated commercial & personal banking models in Mediterranean countries, Türkiye, and Eastern Europe
- **Specialized businesses within CPBS:**
  - **BNP Paribas Personal Finance** (European leader in consumer credit)
  - **Arval** (vehicle leasing and fleet management)
  - **BNP Paribas Leasing Solutions** (equipment and technology financing)
  - **Nickel** (digital banking)
- **Services offered:** financing and equipment leasing, lending, investment products, financial and non-financial services, mobility solutions, digital banking, current accounts, savings products, bancassurance, insurance products, and consumer loans

**Background:** Began career at Banque Nationale de Paris in 1982; served as Chairman and CEO of BNP Paribas Personal Finance (2008–2015); appointed Deputy COO and Head of Domestic Markets in 2015.

---

#### **4. Renaud Dumora – Deputy Chief Operating Officer in charge of Investment & Protection Services (IPS)**

**Responsibilities (appointed May 2021):**
- Heads the **IPS division**, dedicated to **savings, investment, and protection solutions**
- Oversees key businesses:
  - **BNP Paribas Asset Management** (CEO Sandro Pierri reports directly to him)
  - **BNP Paribas Cardif** (insurance subsidiary specializing in personal insurance, creditor insurance, savings, pensions)
  - **BNP Paribas Wealth Management** (private banking and wealth management services)
  - **BNP Paribas Real Estate** (real estate advisory, investment management, property development, transaction services)
- Also serves as **Chairman of BNP Paribas Cardif**
- Provides protection, savings, investment, and real estate services to clients across multiple geographies

**Background:** Began career at Compagnie Bancaire in 1990; joined BNP Paribas Cardif's actuarial department in 1994; became CEO of BNP Paribas Cardif in 2016; graduate of École Polytechnique, ENSAE, and Institut des Actuaires Français.

---

#### **5. Philippe Maillard – Chief Operating Officer (Group COO)**

**Responsibilities:**
- Serves as **Group Chief Operating Officer**
- Oversees cross-functional operations and coordination
- Sarah Roussel (Group Head of Human Resources, appointed July 1, 2026) reports to him

---

### **Executive Committee Composition**

Beyond the General Management, the Executive Committee includes **heads of business lines and central functions**. As of 2026, key members include:

| **Name** | **Responsibility** |
|----------|-------------------|
| **Michael Anseeuw** | Director and CEO / Chairman of the Executive Board, BNP Paribas Fortis |
| **Marc Camus** | Chief Information Officer |
| **Charlotte Dennery** | Director and CEO, BNP Paribas Personal Finance |
| **Elena Goitini** | CEO of BNL (Italy) |
| **Élise Hermant** | Head of Communications |
| **Yannick Jung** | Head of CIB Global Banking |
| **Pauline Leclerc-Glorieux** | Director and CEO, BNP Paribas Cardif |
| **Isabelle Loc** | Head of Commercial & Personal Banking in France |
| **Stéphanie Maarek** | Head of Compliance |
| **Lars Machenil** | Chief Financial Officer |
| **Olivier Osty** | Head of CIB Global Markets |
| **Sandro Pierri** | CEO of BNP Paribas Asset Management (joined Executive Committee March 30, 2026) |
| **Anne Pointet** | Head of Company Engagement |
| **Frank Roncey** | Chief Risk Officer |
| **Sarah Roussel** | Head of Human Resources (appointed July 1, 2026) |
| **Gilles Zeitoun** | Executive Committee member |

---

### **Key Responsibilities of the Executive Committee**

- **Strategy setting and implementation:** Sets and implements BNP Paribas's overall strategy to consolidate European leadership and grow profitably
- **Operational oversight:** Coordinates all operational activities and Group functions across business lines
- **Sustainable economy transition:** Coordinates efforts to accelerate the transition to a sustainable economic model and support clients
- **Diversity and governance:** In 2024, 42% of Executive Committee members were women, exceeding the Group's 40% target by 2025
- **Weekly meetings:** Convenes at least once a week to ensure close coordination

---

This leadership structure enables BNP Paribas to maintain integrated oversight across its three main operating divisions (CIB, CPBS, and IPS) while ensuring strategic alignment and operational excellence across its global operations in 64 countries with nearly 178,000 employees.

query: What is the average CET1 capital ratio and NPL ratio of EU banks in the latest quarter?
answer:
Based on the latest available data from the European Banking Authority (EBA) Risk Dashboard for Q4 2025 (published in March 2026), the average financial metrics for EU/EEA banks are:

**CET1 Capital Ratio:** Approximately **15.8–16.0%** (near record levels)

**NPL Ratio:** **1.8%**

These figures demonstrate that EU banks maintain a robust capital position with capital ratios at near-record levels, driven by strong organic capital growth. The non-performing loan ratio has remained stable at 1.8%, with NPL volumes at approximately €370 billion in Q4 2025.

Additional context:
- Under full CRR3 implementation, the average CET1 ratio is projected to decline slightly to 15.3%, while remaining robust
- The share of Stage 2 loans fell to 9.1% in Q4 2025, indicating improving credit quality
- The ECB noted that overall CET1 requirements and guidance applicable in 2026 are steady at 11.2%, meaning EU/EEA banks hold substantial buffers above minimum requirements

Note: Q4 2025 represents the most recent publicly available data from the EBA Risk Dashboard as of the information provided.

## EU/EEA Banks — Average CET1 Capital Ratio and NPL Ratio (Latest Available Data)

Based on the most recent European Banking Authority (EBA) Risk Dashboard publications:

### Q4 2025 Data (published March 2026)

| Metric | Average |
|---|---|
| **CET1 Capital Ratio** | ~**15.8–16.0%** (near record levels) |
| **NPL Ratio** | **1.8%** |

- Non-performing loan volumes stood at approximately **€370 billion**, with the NPL ratio steady at **1.8%**.
- The share of Stage 2 loans fell to **9.1%**, indicating improving credit quality.
- Under full CRR3 implementation, the average CET1 ratio is projected to decline slightly to **15.3%**, while remaining robust.

### Q3 2025 Data (published December 2025)

| Metric | Average |
|---|---|
| **CET1 Capital Ratio** | Near record levels (capital ratios remained robust) |
| **NPL Ratio** | **1.8%** |

- NPL volumes were broadly stable at **€373 billion**.
- Stage 2 loans continued decreasing slowly to **9.3%**.
- The cost of risk stood at **0.47%**, the lowest since Q3 2023.

### Key Context

- The ECB noted that overall CET1 requirements and guidance applicable in 2026 are steady at **11.2%**, meaning EU/EEA banks hold substantial buffers above minimum requirements.
- European bank profits have remained resilient, with 83% of banks beating pre-tax profit expectations in Q2 2026 earnings, and most upgrading full-year guidance.
- The EBA highlighted that EU/EEA banks maintain a robust capital base with capital ratios near record levels, driven by strong organic capital growth.

**Note:** The latest publicly available EBA Risk Dashboard covers **Q4 2025** data (published in March 2026). The Q1 2026 dashboard had not yet been published as of the most recent available information. The Q2 2026 dashboard is typically expected in autumn 2026.

query: What capital and liquidity (LCR) levels do significant institutions supervised by the ECB report?
answer:
Significant institutions supervised by the European Central Bank (ECB) report strong capital and liquidity levels that are well above regulatory minimums.

## Capital Ratios (Q2 2025)

Based on the most recent published data for the second quarter of 2025:

- **Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio: 16.12%** – up from 16.05% in Q1 2025 and 15.81% one year earlier
- **Tier 1 ratio: 17.60%**
- **Total Capital ratio: 20.24%** – slightly down from 20.29% in Q1 2025

The CET1 ratio varies significantly across countries, ranging from **13.18% in Spain to 23.71% in Latvia** in Q2 2025.

These capital levels provide substantial headroom above regulatory requirements. The overall SREP (Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process) CET1 requirements and guidance, including systemic and countercyclical buffers, stood at approximately **11.7%** as of the 2019 SREP cycle. CET1 ratios have reached new highs, further increasing capital headroom and contributing to banking sector resilience.

## Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR)

- **Aggregate LCR: 157.84%** in Q2 2025, up from 156.24% in Q1 2025

This is well above the regulatory minimum of **100%**. The European Banking Authority's June 2026 Risk Assessment Report expects the sector's LCR to decline modestly to about **155% in 2026**, while remaining comfortably above the minimum requirement.

The ECB publishes these aggregated supervisory banking statistics on a quarterly basis, drawing on harmonized COREP (common reporting) and FINREP (financial reporting) frameworks from banks it directly supervises.

## Capital and Liquidity Levels of ECB-Supervised Significant Institutions

The European Central Bank publishes aggregate supervisory banking statistics on significant institutions (SIs) — the banks it directly supervises — on a quarterly basis, drawing on harmonised COREP and FINREP reporting frameworks.

### Capital Ratios

Based on the most recent published data (Q2 2025, released 17 September 2025):

- **Aggregate CET1 (Common Equity Tier 1) ratio: 16.12%** — up from 16.05% in Q1 2025 and 15.81% a year earlier.
- **Aggregate Tier 1 ratio: 17.60%**
- **Aggregate Total Capital ratio: 20.24%** — slightly down from 20.29% in Q1 2025.

Across countries, the CET1 ratio ranged from **13.18% in Spain to 23.71% in Latvia** in Q2 2025.

For context, the overall SREP CET1 requirements and guidance (including systemic and countercyclical buffers) requested by authorities stood at approximately **11.7%** as of the 2019 SREP cycle, meaning the sector maintains substantial headroom above regulatory minimums. CET1 ratios have been described as reaching a new high, further increasing capital headroom and contributing to banking sector resilience.

### Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR)

- **Aggregate LCR: 157.84%** in Q2 2025, up from 156.24% in Q1 2025.

This is well above the regulatory minimum of **100%**. The EBA's June 2026 Risk Assessment Report expects the sector's LCR to decline modestly to about **155% in 2026**, while remaining comfortably above the minimum.

### Key Takeaways

- Euro area significant institutions hold capital and liquidity buffers significantly above regulatory minimums.
- Capital ratios have been on an upward trend, with CET1 reaching new highs.
- The LCR remains robust at roughly 155–158%, providing ample short-term liquidity coverage.
- The ECB publishes updated supervisory banking statistics quarterly via its Data Portal, with the next update expected to cover more recent quarters.

## Capital Ratios (Q2 2025)

Spain has been the standout performer among major eurozone economies:

- **2023:** Spain significantly outpaced eurozone peers (which grew just 0.4%)
- **2024:** GDP growth was revised upward, with robust expansion far exceeding the eurozone's 0.9%
- **2025:** The economy grew **2.8%** for the full year—more than double the eurozone average of 1.5%. Quarter-on-quarter growth was 0.8% in Q2 and 0.6% in Q3. Spain's total output has risen approximately 10% since 2019, well above the eurozone average of 6.4%
- **2026 forecast:** GDP growth is expected at around **2.1%**, still well above the eurozone average

Key growth drivers include record tourism (approximately 97 million international visitors in 2025), strong immigration fueling labor supply and consumption, low energy costs, rising exports, and dynamic non-tourism services (IT, telecoms, business services). All three major rating agencies—S&P, Moody's, and Fitch—upgraded Spain's sovereign credit rating in September 2025, citing improved economic resilience and balanced growth.

## Inflation (HICP)

Spain's EU-harmonized inflation (HICP) has shown mixed trends:

- Spain's HICP was among the lowest in the eurozone for much of 2024–2025, helped by relatively low energy prices
- By **October 2025**, HICP had risen to **3.2%** year-on-year (up from 3.0% in September), above the 3.0% analysts had expected
- Core inflation stood at **2.5%** in October 2025
- **Industrial prices** surged in early 2026: in **April 2026**, Spanish industrial prices rose **8.3% year-on-year**—the fastest since December 2022—driven mainly by oil refining and chemicals costs, posing an upside risk to consumer inflation

## Unemployment

Spain's unemployment rate remains the highest in the EU but has been on a clear downward trend:

- **Q3 2025:** 10.45%
- **Q4 2025:** **9.93%**—falling below 10% for the first time in years
- **2026 forecast:** approximately **9.8%**

More than half of jobs created since 2020 have been filled by immigrant workers. The 2021 labor reform boosted permanent contracts: in tourism alone, 91.9% of new jobs in 2025 were permanent, and the temporary employment rate fell to 7.6%.

## Summary

Spain's economy is in a strong cyclical position—leading European growth, receiving credit upgrades, and seeing falling unemployment. However, challenges remain: inflation pressures are re-emerging (especially from industrial/energy costs), unemployment is still the EU's highest, housing costs surged nearly 13% in 2025, and GDP per capita gains lag behind headline growth due to immigration-driven population expansion.

{"content":"## Spain HICP Inflation Trend — Recent Years

Spain's Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) has followed a notable trajectory over recent years:

### 2022–2023: Sharp disinflation
After peaking during the 2022 energy crisis, Spain's HICP inflation fell significantly through 2023 as energy prices normalised. By late 2023, the annual HICP rate had come down to around the 3% area (the eurozone-wide headline was at 3.3% in September 2023).

### 2024–2025: Moderate but persistent inflation
- Through much of 2024 and into 2025, Spain's HICP hovered around the **2.5–3.2%** range, remaining above the ECB's 2% target.
- In **October 2025**, Spain's EU-harmonised 12-month inflation rose to **3.2%**, up from 3.0% in September, exceeding the 3.0% analyst consensus. Core inflation (excluding fresh food and energy) stood at **2.5%** year-on-year.

### 2026: Re-acceleration driven by energy
- Inflation has picked up again in 2026, largely driven by surging energy prices (linked in part to geopolitical tensions, including the Iran/Hormuz situation).
- Spain's **industrial prices** rose **8.3% year-on-year in April 2026**, the fastest pace since December 2022, mainly driven by oil refining and chemicals — a leading indicator of consumer price pressures.
- By **August 2026**, eurozone-wide headline HICP hit **3.3%** (the highest since September 2023), with energy inflation at 14.3% year-on-year. Within that, **Spain recorded a 12-month HICP rate of 4.5%** — the highest among the Big Four eurozone economies. Spain's three-month annualised HICP pace reached **7.0%**, though the core rate was more contained at **2.9%** over 12 months and **2.6%** over three months.

### Key takeaway
Spain's HICP inflation followed a disinflationary path from the 2022 peak through 2023–2024, but has re-accelerated in 2025–2026. Energy costs are the primary driver of the latest surge, while core inflation remains elevated but more moderate. Spain currently runs above the eurozone average, partly reflecting strong domestic demand, a booming tourism sector, and pass-through from higher industrial input costs.

## Spain HICP Inflation Trend — Recent Years

Spain's Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) has followed a notable trajectory over recent years:

### 2022–2023: Sharp disinflation
After peaking during the 2022 energy crisis, Spain's HICP inflation fell significantly through 2023 as energy prices normalised. By late 2023, the annual HICP rate had come down to around the 3% area (the eurozone-wide headline was at 3.3% in September 2023).

### 2024–2025: Moderate but persistent inflation
- Through much of 2024 and into 2025, Spain's HICP hovered around the **2.5–3.2%** range, remaining above the ECB's 2% target.
- In **October 2025**, Spain's EU-harmonised 12-month inflation rose to **3.2%**, up from 3.0% in September, exceeding the 3.0% analyst consensus. Core inflation (excluding fresh food and energy) stood at **2.5%** year-on-year.

### 2026: Re-acceleration driven by energy
- Inflation has picked up again in 2026, largely driven by surging energy prices (linked in part to geopolitical tensions, including the Iran/Hormuz situation).
- Spain's **industrial prices** rose **8.3% year-on-year in April 2026**, the fastest pace since December 2022, mainly driven by oil refining and chemicals — a leading indicator of consumer price pressures.
- By **August 2026**, eurozone-wide headline HICP hit **3.3%** (the highest since September 2023), with energy inflation at 14.3% year-on-year. Within that, **Spain recorded a 12-month HICP rate of 4.5%** — the highest among the Big Four eurozone economies. Spain's three-month annualised HICP pace reached **7.0%**, though the core rate was more contained at **2.9%** over 12 months and **2.6%** over three months.

### Key takeaway
Spain's HICP inflation followed a disinflationary path from the 2022 peak through 2023–2024, but has re-accelerated in 2025–2026. Energy costs are the primary driver of the latest surge, while core inflation remains elevated but more moderate. Spain currently runs above the eurozone average, partly reflecting strong domestic demand, a booming tourism sector, and pass-through from higher industrial input costs.

*Latest data referenced: August 2026 (Eurostat flash estimate / Haver Analytics, published 1 September 2026).*

{"content":"## Spain GDP Trend — Recent Years

Spain is the **4th-largest economy in the EU** and the **15th-largest globally**, with a GDP of approximately **$1.72 trillion**. Over recent years, Spain has consistently outperformed its eurozone peers in economic growth:

### Annual GDP Growth

| Year | GDP Growth (%) | Key Context |
|------|---------------|-------------|
| **2023** | ~2.7% | Strong post-pandemic rebound; tourism surged (+10.5% in tourism GDP) |
| **2024** | ~2.8% | Fuelled by consumer demand, rising exports, and robust tourism (+5.5% tourism GDP growth) |
| **2025** | **2.8%** | Government and Bank of Spain forecast 2.7–2.9%; more than double the eurozone average of ~1.2% |
| **2026 (forecast)** | **~2.1–2.2%** | Q1 2026 came in at 2.7% YoY; Q2 2026 at 0.7% quarter-on-quarter — still the fastest among large eurozone economies |

### Key Growth Drivers

- **Tourism**: 2025 was a record year — nearly 97 million overseas visitors, with tourism contributing €218.5 billion (13% of GDP).
- **Immigration & labour market**: More than half of jobs created since 2020 were filled by immigrants, boosting overall output. Unemployment has fallen to ~10.5%.
- **Non-tourism services**: Business, telecoms, and IT services have diversified Spain's growth beyond traditional sectors.
- **Low energy costs & competitiveness**: Moderate wage growth and relatively low energy prices have strengthened external competitiveness.

### Credit Rating Upgrades

In September 2025, Spain received a **triple credit rating upgrade** from all three major agencies:
- **S&P Global**: Cited "notable improvement" in Spain's balance sheet
- **Moody's**: Upgraded to A3, citing economic strength and banking sector resilience
- **Fitch**: Upgraded to A, highlighting productivity gains and external competitiveness

### Caveats

- Spain's GDP output has risen **10% since 2019**, well above the eurozone average of 6.4%. However, much of this growth is driven by population expansion through immigration, meaning **GDP per capita has advanced less strongly**.
- Unemployment at ~10.5% remains the **highest in the EU**.
- Industrial prices rose 8.3% year-on-year in April 2026, and inflation climbed to 3.5–3.6% by mid-2026, posing a potential headwind.

## Spain GDP Trend — Recent Years

Spain is the **4th-largest economy in the EU** and the **15th-largest globally**, with a GDP of approximately **$1.72 trillion**. Over recent years, Spain has consistently outperformed its eurozone peers in economic growth:

### Annual GDP Growth

| Year | GDP Growth (%) | Key Context |
|------|---------------|-------------|
| **2023** | ~2.7% | Strong post-pandemic rebound; tourism surged (+10.5% in tourism GDP) |
| **2024** | ~2.8% | Fuelled by consumer demand, rising exports, and robust tourism (+5.5% tourism GDP growth) |
| **2025** | **2.8%** | Government and Bank of Spain forecast 2.7–2.9%; more than double the eurozone average of ~1.2% |
| **2026 (forecast)** | **~2.1–2.2%** | Q1 2026 came in at 2.7% YoY; Q2 2026 at 0.7% quarter-on-quarter — still the fastest among large eurozone economies |

### Key Growth Drivers

- **Tourism**: 2025 was a record year — nearly 97 million overseas visitors, with tourism contributing €218.5 billion (13% of GDP).
- **Immigration & labour market**: More than half of jobs created since 2020 were filled by immigrants, boosting overall output. Unemployment has fallen to ~10.5%.
- **Non-tourism services**: Business, telecoms, and IT services have diversified Spain's growth beyond traditional sectors.
- **Low energy costs & competitiveness**: Moderate wage growth and relatively low energy prices have strengthened external competitiveness.

### Credit Rating Upgrades

In September 2025, Spain received a **triple credit rating upgrade** from all three major agencies:
- **S&P Global**: Cited "notable improvement" in Spain's balance sheet
- **Moody's**: Upgraded to A3, citing economic strength and banking sector resilience
- **Fitch**: Upgraded to A, highlighting productivity gains and external competitiveness

### Caveats

- Spain's GDP output has risen **10% since 2019**, well above the eurozone average of 6.4%. However, much of this growth is driven by population expansion through immigration, meaning **GDP per capita has advanced less strongly**.
- Unemployment at ~10.5% remains the **highest in the EU**.
- Industrial prices rose 8.3% year-on-year in April 2026, and inflation climbed to 3.5–3.6% by mid-2026, posing a potential headwind.

Overall, Spain has been the **standout growth story** in the eurozone since 2021, though analysts note the growth model is more "extensive" (population-driven) than "intensive" (productivity-driven).

Compared to other EU countries, it is true that Spain’s GDP growth has been extraordinario in recent years. CaixaBank, the country’s largest domestic lender, reported earlier this week that Spain’s output has risen 10% since 2019, well above the eurozone average of 6.4% and a whopping one hundred times more than Germany’s anaemic 0.1% expansion.

The swift growth also shows little sign of subsiding. Earlier this month, the European Commission and the Bank of Spain both hiked their Spanish growth forecasts for this year to 2.9% – more than double the EU’s 1.4% average projected expansion. “Real GDP growth is expected to remain strong in 2025,” the Commission noted, adding that “economic activity” is also expected to “remain robust” until 2027. [...] The wave of immigration has also made it increasingly difficult for Spain to reduce its overall rate of joblessness, which at 10.45% remains the highest in the EU. Nine in ten jobs created between January 2024 and March 2025 were filled by foreign workers, the Elcano Institute notes. Many Spaniards who are employed have seen tepid real wage growth for decades, constricting their buying power – and in many cases their motivation.

Such factors explain why Spain’s economic “miracle” is overwhelmingly not being felt by its citizens. A recent poll by the Funcas research centre revealed that 55% of Spaniards think that the economic situation is worse than before the pandemic, while 90% believe they have lost purchasing power.

## Luzat the end of the tunnel? [...] But as José Boscá, an economist at the FEDEA think tank in Madrid, points out, Spain’s GDP data “is not so promising” when adjusted for its population growth, which has also swelled in recent years. “If we only assess economic growth based on GDP data, there are factors that we are not taking into consideration,” Boscá said.

Indeed, Spain’s GDP growth is largely a direct consequence of its growing population. Soaring immigration – especially from Latin America – has caused Spain’s overall population to surge in recent years, and, predictably, has also caused its total output and consumption to rise.

# 2025 WAS THE GOLDEN YEAR OF SPANISH TOURISM

Sara Thopson - Jan 18, 2026

0

Spain's tourism industry leads the national economy and finished 2025 with record results. Exceltur, the Alliance for Tourism Excellence, released a new report according to which the sector added 218,459 million euros to the economy. This equals 13% of GDP and is a new high. Growth reached 2.5% year-on-year which was however slower than the 5.5% rate in 2024 and the 10.5% rate in 2023. [...] Exceltur predicts that the growth will continue in 2026 but will slow down. They expect the sector to add 229,372 million euros to the economy which is a 2.4% rise. That figure is slightly above the expected Spanish GDP growth of 2.2%. Tourism will make up 13.1% of the total economy. Business owners expect sales to rise by 3.9%, which is less than the 4% rate in 2025. They also expect results to improve by 5.9%. [...] The year marked a change toward what Exceltur calls a smarter, better growth model. Óscar Perelli serves as executive vice-president of Exceltur. He noted that Spanish tourism led the national rise in labor productivity with a 3.8% increase. The Spanish average was 2.8%. Employment rose by 47,815 workers (+2.3%). Permanent contracts made up 91.9% of these new jobs. The temporary employment rate fell to 7.6%, which is well below the national average of 12.3%. Wages also increased. Collective bargaining agreements provided a 3.9% average raise. This rate beat 2025 inflation and gave workers real gains in purchasing power.

{"content":"## Spain — Key Macroeconomic Trends (2023–2026)

### GDP Growth

Spain has been the standout performer among major eurozone economies in recent years:

- **2023:** Eurozone GDP grew just 0.4%, with Spain significantly outpacing peers.
- **2024:** Spain's GDP growth was revised upward, with the economy expanding robustly. The eurozone managed only 0.9%.
- **2025:** Spain's economy grew **2.8%** for the full year — more than double the eurozone average of 1.5%. Quarter-on-quarter growth was 0.8% in Q2 and 0.6% in Q3. The government and Bank of Spain had raised their 2025 forecast to **2.7%**, but the final outturn exceeded even that. Spain's total output has risen roughly 10% since 2019, well above the eurozone average of 6.4%.
- **2026 forecast:** GDP growth is expected at around **2.1%**, still well above the eurozone average.

Key growth drivers include booming tourism (a record ~97 million international visitors in 2025), strong immigration fuelling labour supply and consumption, low energy costs, rising exports, and dynamic non-tourism services (IT, telecoms, business services). All three major rating agencies — S&P, Moody's, and Fitch — upgraded Spain's sovereign credit rating in September 2025, citing improved economic resilience and balanced growth.

### Inflation (HICP)

- Spain's EU-harmonised inflation (HICP) was among the lowest in the eurozone for much of 2024–2025, helped by relatively low energy prices.
- By **October 2025**, HICP had risen to **3.2%** year-on-year (up from 3.0% in September), above the 3.0% analysts had expected. Core inflation stood at **2.5%**.
- **Industrial prices** surged in early 2026: in **April 2026**, Spanish industrial prices rose **8.3% year-on-year** — the fastest since December 2022 — driven mainly by oil refining and chemicals costs. This poses an upside risk to consumer inflation going forward.
- Eurozone-wide, the ECB expects inflation to decline back toward the 2% target by around 2027–2028, but energy-related pressures remain a near-term concern.

### Unemployment

- Spain's unemployment rate remains the **highest in the EU**, but has been on a clear downward trend:
  - **Q3 2025:** 10.45%
  - **Q4 2025:** **9.93%** — falling below 10% for the first time in years.
  - **2026 forecast:** approximately **9.8%**.
- More than half of jobs created since 2020 have been filled by immigrant workers. The 2021 labour reform boosted permanent contracts: in tourism alone, 91.9% of new jobs in 2025 were permanent, and the temporary employment rate fell to 7.6%.
- Despite headline improvements, real wage growth has been tepid for many Spaniards, and GDP per capita has advanced less strongly than total GDP due to rapid population growth.

### Summary

Spain's economy is in a strong cyclical position — leading European growth, receiving credit upgrades, and seeing falling unemployment. However, challenges remain: inflation pressures are re-emerging (especially from industrial/energy costs), unemployment is still the EU's highest, housing costs surged nearly 13% in 2025, and GDP per capita gains lag behind headline growth due to immigration-driven population expansion.

# Spain's 12-month EU-harmonised inflation rises to 3.2% in October

RefinitivLess than 1 min read

Spain's European Union-harmonised 12-month inflation rate rose to 3.2% in October, from 3.0% in the period through September, preliminary data from the National Statistics Institute (INE) showed on Thursday.

The 12-month EU-harmonised inflation was above the 3.0% expected by analysts polled by Reuters.

Core inflation, which strips out volatile fresh food and energy prices, was 2.5% year-on-year, INE's data showed.

Spain's 12-month national inflation was 3.1%, up from 3.0% in September. Analysts polled by Reuters had expected a 2.9% rate.

## Spain — Key Macroeconomic Trends (2023–2026)

### GDP Growth

Spain has been the standout performer among major eurozone economies in recent years:

- **2023:** Eurozone GDP grew just 0.4%, with Spain significantly outpacing peers.
- **2024:** Spain's GDP growth was revised upward, with the economy expanding robustly. The eurozone managed only 0.9%.
- **2025:** Spain's economy grew **2.8%** for the full year — more than double the eurozone average of 1.5%. Quarter-on-quarter growth was 0.8% in Q2 and 0.6% in Q3. The government and Bank of Spain had raised their 2025 forecast to **2.7%**, but the final outturn exceeded even that. Spain's total output has risen roughly 10% since 2019, well above the eurozone average of 6.4%.
- **2026 forecast:** GDP growth is expected at around **2.1%**, still well above the eurozone average.

Key growth drivers include booming tourism (a record ~97 million international visitors in 2025), strong immigration fuelling labour supply and consumption, low energy costs, rising exports, and dynamic non-tourism services (IT, telecoms, business services). All three major rating agencies — S&P, Moody's, and Fitch — upgraded Spain's sovereign credit rating in September 2025, citing improved economic resilience and balanced growth.

### Inflation (HICP)

- Spain's EU-harmonised inflation (HICP) was among the lowest in the eurozone for much of 2024–2025, helped by relatively low energy prices.
- By **October 2025**, HICP had risen to **3.2%** year-on-year (up from 3.0% in September), above the 3.0% analysts had expected. Core inflation stood at **2.5%**.
- **Industrial prices** surged in early 2026: in **April 2026**, Spanish industrial prices rose **8.3% year-on-year** — the fastest since December 2022 — driven mainly by oil refining and chemicals costs. This poses an upside risk to consumer inflation going forward.
- Eurozone-wide, the ECB expects inflation to decline back toward the 2% target by around 2027–2028, but energy-related pressures remain a near-term concern.

### Unemployment

- Spain's unemployment rate remains the **highest in the EU**, but has been on a clear downward trend:
  - **Q3 2025:** 10.45%
  - **Q4 2025:** **9.93%** — falling below 10% for the first time in years.
  - **2026 forecast:** approximately **9.8%**.
- More than half of jobs created since 2020 have been filled by immigrant workers. The 2021 labour reform boosted permanent contracts: in tourism alone, 91.9% of new jobs in 2025 were permanent, and the temporary employment rate fell to 7.6%.
- Despite headline improvements, real wage growth has been tepid for many Spaniards, and GDP per capita has advanced less strongly than total GDP due to rapid population growth.

### Summary

Spain's economy is in a strong cyclical position — leading European growth, receiving credit upgrades, and seeing falling unemployment. However, challenges remain: inflation pressures are re-emerging (especially from industrial/energy costs), unemployment is still the EU's highest, housing costs surged nearly 13% in 2025, and GDP per capita gains lag behind headline growth due to immigration-driven population expansion.

Compared to other EU countries, it is true that Spain’s GDP growth has been extraordinario in recent years. CaixaBank, the country’s largest domestic lender, reported earlier this week that Spain’s output has risen 10% since 2019, well above the eurozone average of 6.4% and a whopping one hundred times more than Germany’s anaemic 0.1% expansion.

The swift growth also shows little sign of subsiding. Earlier this month, the European Commission and the Bank of Spain both hiked their Spanish growth forecasts for this year to 2.9% – more than double the EU’s 1.4% average projected expansion. “Real GDP growth is expected to remain strong in 2025,” the Commission noted, adding that “economic activity” is also expected to “remain robust” until 2027. [...] The wave of immigration has also made it increasingly difficult for Spain to reduce its overall rate of joblessness, which at 10.45% remains the highest in the EU. Nine in ten jobs created between January 2024 and March 2025 were filled by foreign workers, the Elcano Institute notes. Many Spaniards who are employed have seen tepid real wage growth for decades, constricting their buying power – and in many cases their motivation.

Such factors explain why Spain’s economic “miracle” is overwhelmingly not being felt by its citizens. A recent poll by the Funcas research centre revealed that 55% of Spaniards think that the economic situation is worse than before the pandemic, while 90% believe they have lost purchasing power.

## Luzat the end of the tunnel? [...] But as José Boscá, an economist at the FEDEA think tank in Madrid, points out, Spain’s GDP data “is not so promising” when adjusted for its population growth, which has also swelled in recent years. “If we only assess economic growth based on GDP data, there are factors that we are not taking into consideration,” Boscá said.

Indeed, Spain’s GDP growth is largely a direct consequence of its growing population. Soaring immigration – especially from Latin America – has caused Spain’s overall population to surge in recent years, and, predictably, has also caused its total output and consumption to rise.

Spain's economy has shown strong positive trends across key macroeconomic indicators in recent years:

## GDP Growth

Spain has been the standout performer among major eurozone economies:

- **2023:** Spain significantly outpaced eurozone peers (which grew just 0.4%)
- **2024:** GDP growth was revised upward, with robust expansion far exceeding the eurozone's 0.9%
- **2025:** The economy grew **2.8%** for the full year—more than double the eurozone average of 1.5%. Quarter-on-quarter growth was 0.8% in Q2 and 0.6% in Q3. Spain's total output has risen approximately 10% since 2019, well above the eurozone average of 6.4%
- **2026 forecast:** GDP growth is expected at around **2.1%**, still well above the eurozone average

Key growth drivers include record tourism (approximately 97 million international visitors in 2025), strong immigration fueling labor supply and consumption, low energy costs, rising exports, and dynamic non-tourism services (IT, telecoms, business services). All three major rating agencies—S&P, Moody's, and Fitch—upgraded Spain's sovereign credit rating in September 2025, citing improved economic resilience and balanced growth.

## Inflation (HICP)

Spain's EU-harmonized inflation (HICP) has shown mixed trends:

- Spain's HICP was among the lowest in the eurozone for much of 2024–2025, helped by relatively low energy prices
- By **October 2025**, HICP had risen to **3.2%** year-on-year (up from 3.0% in September), above the 3.0% analysts had expected
- Core inflation stood at **2.5%** in October 2025
- **Industrial prices** surged in early 2026: in **April 2026**, Spanish industrial prices rose **8.3% year-on-year**—the fastest since December 2022—driven mainly by oil refining and chemicals costs, posing an upside risk to consumer inflation

## Unemployment

Spain's unemployment rate remains the highest in the EU but has been on a clear downward trend:

- **Q3 2025:** 10.45%
- **Q4 2025:** **9.93%**—falling below 10% for the first time in years
- **2026 forecast:** approximately **9.8%**

More than half of jobs created since 2020 have been filled by immigrant workers. The 2021 labor reform boosted permanent contracts: in tourism alone, 91.9% of new jobs in 2025 were permanent, and the temporary employment rate fell to 7.6%.

## Summary

Spain's economy is in a strong cyclical position—leading European growth, receiving credit upgrades, and seeing falling unemployment. However, challenges remain: inflation pressures are re-emerging (especially from industrial/energy costs), unemployment is still the EU's highest, housing costs surged nearly 13% in 2025, and GDP per capita gains lag behind headline growth due to immigration-driven population expansion.

The ECB's **deposit facility rate** currently stands at **2.25%**, following a 25-basis-point increase in June 2026. This was the first rate hike since 2023, implemented in response to an energy-price shock driven by the U.S.-Israel-Iran conflict and resulting surge in oil prices.

The most recent M3 data available is for **May 2026**, showing:

- **M1 growth: 5.1%**, reflecting stronger liquidity
- **Loans to households: 2.0%** annual growth
- **Corporate lending: 2.5%** annual growth

The narrower M1 aggregate has shown even stronger momentum, suggesting improved consumer and business confidence.

## ECB Official Interest Rate — Current Status and Outlook (as of 8 September 2026)

### Current Rate
The ECB's **deposit facility rate** currently stands at **2.25%**, following a 25-basis-point hike in **June 2026** — the first rate increase since 2023.

### Timeline of Recent Decisions
- **June 2025 → June 2026:** The ECB held the deposit rate steady at **2.00%** for roughly a year after completing a cutting cycle that brought the rate down from 4%.
- **June 2026:** The ECB raised the rate by 25 bps to **2.25%**, responding to an energy-price shock driven by the U.S.-Israel-Iran conflict and the resulting surge in oil prices.
- **July 2026:** The ECB held at 2.25%, though some Governing Council members were already open to another hike.

### Upcoming Decision — 10 September 2026
Markets have **fully priced in** a second 25-basis-point hike at the ECB's meeting on **Thursday, 10 September**, which would bring the deposit rate to **2.50%**. Key factors:

- **Eurozone inflation** rose back above **3%** in August (3.3% headline), driven by elevated energy prices.
- ECB President Christine Lagarde has warned that inflation will remain "well above target" until the first half of 2027.
- The meeting will also include updated ECB macroeconomic projections.

### What Comes After September?
- **Most economists** polled by Reuters expect the ECB to stop hiking after September, viewing 2.50% as the top end of the neutral range.
- However, **Deutsche Bank, J.P. Morgan, and BNP Paribas** now forecast an additional hike in **December 2026**, which would take the rate to 2.75%, citing persistent energy risks.
- ING describes the expected September move as an "insurance hike" — a precautionary step to preserve credibility and pre-empt second-round inflation effects.
- There is **little evidence so far** of energy-driven inflation broadening into wages, which limits the case for aggressive further tightening.

### What is M3?

M3 is the European Central Bank's preferred broad measure of money supply. It comprises:
- **M1**: currency in circulation plus overnight deposits
- **M2**: M1 plus deposits with an agreed maturity up to 2 years and deposits redeemable at up to 3 months' notice
- **M3**: M2 plus marketable instruments (repurchase agreements, money market fund shares, and debt securities up to 2 years)

The ECB historically set a 4.5% reference growth rate for M3 (3-month moving average, year-over-year), though the significance of this target has been downgraded over time.

### Latest Reported Figures

Based on the most recent available data releases:

- **May 2026**: M3 annual growth rate was **3.8%**, with a consensus expectation of 4.0% for June 2026. The M1 aggregate accelerated to 5.1%, reflecting stronger liquidity. Loans to households grew at 2.0%, while corporate lending softened slightly to 2.5%.

- **January 2026**: M3 annual growth was **3.7%** (up from 3.6% in December 2025), with the 3-month moving average at **2.9%**. Private sector lending stood at 3.1%.

### Trend Summary

M3 growth has been on a gradual upward trajectory — from around 3.0% in late 2025 to approximately 3.8% by mid-2026 — reflecting increased liquidity in the euro area economy. The narrower M1 aggregate has shown even stronger momentum, suggesting improved consumer and business confidence. Credit conditions have been broadly supportive, though corporate lending has shown some signs of softening in recent months.

> **Note:** The ECB typically publishes M3 data with a roughly one-month lag. The latest fully reported figure available is for **May 2026** (released late June 2026). The June/July 2026 data may have been published more recently but was not captured in the sources reviewed.

answer:
## Federal Funds Rate and US Unemployment Rate Evolution (Last 24 Months)

### Federal Funds Rate (September 2024 - September 2026)

The federal funds rate has undergone significant changes over the past 24 months, moving through distinct phases:

**2024: Beginning of the Easing Cycle**
- Prior to September 2024, the rate had been held at 5.25%–5.50% since July 2023
- September 2024: The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) initiated its first rate cut of the cycle, reducing the rate by 50 basis points to 4.75%–5.00%

**2025: Continued Rate Cuts**
- September 17, 2025: Cut by 25 basis points to 4.00%–4.25%
- October 29, 2025: Cut by 25 basis points to 3.75%–4.00%
- December 10, 2025: Cut by 25 basis points to 3.50%–3.75% (third consecutive reduction)

**2026: Rate Holds and Potential Reversal**
- January–June 2026: The rate was held steady at 3.50%–3.75% across multiple meetings
- June 17, 2026: First meeting under new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh maintained the 3.50%–3.75% range, but the updated dot plot showed the median year-end estimate rising to 3.8%, with several officials penciling in at least one rate hike
- As of September 8, 2026: The rate remains at 3.50%–3.75%, with markets pricing in approximately 58–60% probability of a 25 basis point hike at the September 15-16, 2026 meeting

**Summary**: Over the 24-month period, the federal funds rate declined from 5.25%–5.50% to 3.50%–3.75%, representing a total reduction of 175 basis points through a series of cuts, followed by a nine-month pause with potential tightening on the horizon.

### US Unemployment Rate (September 2024 - August 2026)

The unemployment rate has shown a pattern of gradual increase followed by stabilization:

**Late 2024**
- September–December 2024: The rate remained relatively stable, hovering around 4.1%–4.2%

**2025: Gradual Deterioration**
- January–May 2025: The rate held steady at approximately 4.0%–4.1%
- June–July 2025: Increased to 4.2%
- August 2025: Rose to 4.3%
- September 2025: Climbed to 4.4%
- October 2025: Estimated at approximately 4.4% (Chicago Fed estimate; BLS data was disrupted by a 43-day government shutdown)
- November 2025: Reached a four-year high of 4.6%
- December 2025: Declined to 4.4%

**2026: Stabilization and Modest Improvement**
- January–May 2026: Stabilized at approximately 4.3%
- June 2026: Declined to approximately 4.2%
- July–August 2026: Further improved to 4.1%

**Key Factors**: The unemployment rate increase in 2025 was driven by sweeping import tariffs, federal workforce reductions, reduced immigration, and lingering effects of high interest rates. Total US job growth in 2025 was only approximately 584,000 (averaging about 49,000 jobs per month), far below 2024's roughly 2 million additions. In 2026, the labor market entered a "low-hire, low-fire" equilibrium, with reduced immigration and Baby Boomer retirements shrinking the labor force and lowering the break-even rate for job creation to roughly 0–50,000 jobs per month.

**Summary**: The unemployment rate rose from approximately 4.1% in late 2024 to a peak of 4.6% in November 2025, then stabilized and improved to approximately 4.1% by mid-2026, representing a relatively modest fluctuation within a narrow range.

## Federal Funds Rate Evolution — Last 24 Months (Sep 2024 – Sep 2026)

Below is a timeline of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) decisions on the federal funds target range over the past two years:

### 2024: Easing Cycle Begins
| Meeting | Decision | Target Range |
|---|---|---|
| Sep 2024 | **First cut of the cycle** (–50 bps) | 4.75%–5.00% |
| (Prior to Sep 2024 the rate had been held at 5.25%–5.50% since Jul 2023) |

### 2025: Continued Cuts, Then a Pause
| Meeting | Decision | Target Range |
|---|---|---|
| Sep 17, 2025 | **Cut 25 bps** | 4.00%–4.25% |
| Oct 29, 2025 | **Cut 25 bps** | 3.75%–4.00% |
| Dec 10, 2025 | **Cut 25 bps** (third straight cut) | 3.50%–3.75% |

The September 2025 dot plot projected only one additional cut in 2026, with the median year-end 2026 estimate at 3.4%. Fed Chair Jerome Powell, in his final meetings before his term expired in May 2026, described the economy as "extraordinary" while noting inflation remained somewhat elevated.

### 2026: Rate Holds — and a Possible Hike Looms
| Meeting | Decision | Target Range |
|---|---|---|
| Jan–Jun 2026 (multiple meetings) | **Held steady** | 3.50%–3.75% |
| Jun 17, 2026 | **Held steady** — first meeting under new Chair Kevin Warsh. The updated dot plot showed the median year-end estimate rising to 3.8%, with several officials penciling in at least one rate **hike** in 2026. | 3.50%–3.75% |

### Current Situation (as of Sep 8, 2026)
- The federal funds target range remains at **3.50%–3.75%**, unchanged since December 2025.
- The next FOMC meeting is scheduled for **September 15–16, 2026**, and a potential **rate hike** is actively being debated.
- Markets are pricing in roughly a **58–60% probability** of a 25 bps hike to 3.75%–4.00% at the September meeting, following a strong August jobs report (+162,000 jobs, unemployment steady at 4.1%) and hawkish signals from Chair Warsh at Jackson Hole.
- Fed Governor Christopher Waller has indicated he would support holding rates if August inflation data (CPI due Sep 11) shows continued progress toward 2%, but would consider a hike if inflation "comes in hot."
- UBS, Bank of America, and Macquarie have all shifted their forecasts to expect at least one rate hike in September, with some forecasting a second hike later in 2026 or early 2027.

### Summary
Over the last 24 months, the federal funds rate has moved from **5.25%–5.50%** (mid-2024) down to **3.50%–3.75%** (Dec 2025) through a series of cuts, and has been on hold at that level for nine months. The policy stance may now be shifting toward tightening, with the September 2026 meeting representing a potential inflection point.

## The Path For Interest Rates In 2026

By December 2026, the Federal Funds rate is expected to be around 3% that’s down from the current range of 3.75% to 4%. However, the range of outcomes is broad and rates could move as low as 2% or remain as high as 4% according to the more extreme outliers of fixed income market estimates. To the extent the FOMC does cut rates, the bulk of cuts may come in the first half of 2026. Policymakers’ own projections for rates in 2026 are a little more modest, with rates seen as remaining above 3% on most estimates. However, these projections were last updated in September and will be revised again in December.

## The FOMC’s 2026 Meeting Calendar [...] ## A New Fed Chair

President Trump is expected to nominate a Federal Reserve Chair to take office in 2026 who supports his drive for lower interest rates. Prediction markets, such as Kalshi, currently view Kevin Hassett as the most likely nominee. This may add impetus for lower rates in 2026. For example, Trump appointed Stephen Miran during 2025 and he has been consistent, so far, in voting for aggressively for lower rates. However, despite an expected new Fed Chair, the composition of the FOMC will remain broadly similar to past years. That means that monetary policy may not change too much because of a new Fed Chair.

{"content":"## U.S. Unemployment Rate — Last 24 Months (Sep 2024 – Aug 2026)

Below is a month-by-month reconstruction of the U.S. unemployment rate over the past ~24 months, based on Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) releases and related reports:

### 2024 (latter half)
| Month | Unemployment Rate |
|-------|:-:|
| Sep 2024 | ~4.1% |
| Oct 2024 | ~4.1% |
| Nov 2024 | ~4.2% |
| Dec 2024 | ~4.1% |

The labor market in late 2024 was relatively stable, with the unemployment rate hovering around 4.1–4.2%.

### 2025 — A Year of Gradual Deterioration
| Month | Unemployment Rate |
|-------|:-:|
| Jan 2025 | ~4.0% |
| Feb 2025 | ~4.1% |
| Mar 2025 | ~4.1% |
| Apr 2025 | ~4.1% |
| May 2025 | ~4.1% |
| Jun 2025 | ~4.2% |
| Jul 2025 | ~4.2% |
| Aug 2025 | 4.3% |
| Sep 2025 | 4.4% |
| Oct 2025 | ~4.4% (Chicago Fed estimate; BLS data disrupted by government shutdown) |
| Nov 2025 | 4.6% (four-year high) |
| Dec 2025 | 4.4% |

The unemployment rate drifted steadily higher throughout 2025, reaching a four-year high of 4.6% in November. Key headwinds included sweeping import tariffs, a federal workforce purge, reduced immigration, and the lingering effects of high interest rates. A 43-day government shutdown disrupted BLS data collection, meaning October 2025 data was estimated by the Chicago Fed rather than officially published.

### 2026 — Stabilization
| Month | Unemployment Rate |
|-------|:-:|
| Jan 2026 | 4.3% |
| Feb 2026 | ~4.3% |
| Mar 2026 | 4.3% |
| Apr 2026 | ~4.3% |
| May 2026 | 4.3% |
| Jun 2026 | ~4.2% |
| Jul 2026 | 4.1% |
| Aug 2026 | ~4.1% (forecast; official report due Sep 2026) |

In 2026, the unemployment rate has stabilized and gradually declined from 4.3% back toward 4.1%, as the labor market entered a "low-hire, low-fire" equilibrium. Employers have been reluctant to lay off workers but also cautious about new hiring amid ongoing geopolitical and trade uncertainties. Reduced immigration and Baby Boomer retirements have shrunk the labor force, lowering the break-even rate for job creation to roughly 0–50,000 jobs per month.

### Key Takeaways
- **Peak**: 4.6% in November 2025 — the highest since late 2021.
- **Current level**: ~4.1% as of July 2026 (latest official BLS release); August 2026 data is expected to hold steady at 4.1%.
- **Trend**: The rate rose through most of 2025 due to tariffs, federal workforce cuts, and slowing hiring, then stabilized and modestly improved in 2026.
- Total U.S. job growth in 2025 was only ~584,000 (avg. ~49,000/month), far below 2024's ~2 million additions.

## U.S. Unemployment Rate — Last 24 Months (Sep 2024 – Aug 2026)

Below is a month-by-month reconstruction of the U.S. unemployment rate over the past ~24 months, based on Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) releases and related reports:

### 2024 (latter half)
| Month | Unemployment Rate |
|-------|:-:|
| Sep 2024 | ~4.1% |
| Oct 2024 | ~4.1% |
| Nov 2024 | ~4.2% |
| Dec 2024 | ~4.1% |

The labor market in late 2024 was relatively stable, with the unemployment rate hovering around 4.1–4.2%.

### 2025 — A Year of Gradual Deterioration
| Month | Unemployment Rate |
|-------|:-:|
| Jan 2025 | ~4.0% |
| Feb 2025 | ~4.1% |
| Mar 2025 | ~4.1% |
| Apr 2025 | ~4.1% |
| May 2025 | ~4.1% |
| Jun 2025 | ~4.2% |
| Jul 2025 | ~4.2% |
| Aug 2025 | 4.3% |
| Sep 2025 | 4.4% |
| Oct 2025 | ~4.4% (Chicago Fed estimate; BLS data disrupted by government shutdown) |
| Nov 2025 | 4.6% (four-year high) |
| Dec 2025 | 4.4% |

The unemployment rate drifted steadily higher throughout 2025, reaching a four-year high of 4.6% in November. Key headwinds included sweeping import tariffs, a federal workforce purge, reduced immigration, and the lingering effects of high interest rates. A 43-day government shutdown disrupted BLS data collection, meaning October 2025 data was estimated by the Chicago Fed rather than officially published.

### 2026 — Stabilization
| Month | Unemployment Rate |
|-------|:-:|
| Jan 2026 | 4.3% |

In 2026, the unemployment rate has stabilized and gradually declined from 4.3% back toward 4.1%, as the labor market entered a "low-hire, low-fire" equilibrium.
